claims.text: Increasing lattice distortion in multiprincipal-element alloys raises vacancy formation energy.
Increasing lattice distortion raises the migration barrier for aluminum.
Higher vacancy-formation and aluminum-migration barriers suppress diffusion from the alloy to the oxidation front.
Lattice-distortion-induced diffusion suppression reduces sustained oxide-scale growth.
Diffusion suppression itself promotes rapid initial formation of a protective Al2O3 scale.
The resulting Al2O3 scale is uniform and adherent.
Slower oxide growth and an adherent protective scale preserve material integrity at high temperature.
Adding elements with greater atomic-size discrepancy, or increasing their concentration, will increase lattice distortion.
A comparable alloy with lower lattice distortion will have faster oxide growth and more scale spallation.
At approximately 1200 degrees Celsius for 500 hours, the higher-distortion alloy will have a lower TGO growth rate than the baseline.
The reduction in TGO growth rate could be on the order of tens of percent or more.
The higher-distortion alloy will show less oxide-scale spallation than the baseline.
The higher-distortion alloy will show improved oxide-scale or coating adhesion.
The higher-distortion alloy will have fewer defects at the oxide/alloy interface.
A 1200 degrees Celsius, 500-hour oxidation exposure is relevant to assessing this mechanism.
The mechanism should apply broadly to aluminum-bearing multiprincipal-element alloys near 1200 degrees Celsius during prolonged exposure.
Outside the stated temperature and duration range, or in alloys lacking a protective-oxide-forming reactive element, lattice-distortion-induced diffusion suppression may not dominate oxidation.
Other alloying elements and microstructural factors can influence oxidation kinetics and scale integrity.
Failure of the modified alloy to improve oxide growth rate, adhesion, or spallation relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says that inhibiting aluminum migration promotes rapid formation of Al2O3, while the mechanism says that aluminum transport to the oxidation front is made more difficult. These can coexist only if a distinct initial-stage formation pathway is specified. The cited study assigns rapid initial scale formation to a refined eutectic structure and sustained growth suppression to lattice distortion, but the hypothesis conflates the two effects.
